title: Chapter 58 — Brit
paragraphs: Steering northeast from the Crozets, we fell in with vast meadows of brit, the minute, yellow substance upon which the Right Whale largely feeds. For league upon league it undulated around us, so that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe, golden wheat.

On the second day, numbers of Right Whales were seen, who — safe from the attack of a Sperm Whaler like the Pequod — with open jaws sluggishly swam through the brit. It clung to the fringing fibers of that wondrous Venetian blind in their mouths, and was in this way separated from the water that escaped at the lip.

Like mowers in the morning who move side by side, slowly and seethingly sweeping their scythes through the long wet grass of marshy meadows, these monsters swam along, making a strange, grassy, cutting sound and leaving endless swaths of blue behind them on the yellow sea.*

*That part of the sea known among whalemen as the "Brazil Banks" does not bear that name because of shallows and soundings there, as the Banks of Newfoundland do, but because of this remarkable meadow-like appearance, caused by the vast drifts of brit continually floating in those latitudes, where the Right Whale is often hunted.

But it was only the sound they made as they parted the brit that reminded one of mowers at all. Seen from the mastheads, especially when they paused and were still for a while, their vast black forms looked more like lifeless masses of rock than anything else. And as in the great hunting countries of India the stranger at a distance will sometimes pass elephants lying on the plains without knowing them for what they are, taking them for bare, blackened rises of the ground, so it often is with anyone who sees this species of the leviathans of the sea for the first time. And even when they are recognized at last, their immense size makes it very hard really to believe that such bulky masses of overgrowth can possibly be alive, in every part, with the same sort of life that lives in a dog or a horse.

Indeed, in other ways too, you can hardly feel about any creature of the deep the way you feel about those of the shore. Some old naturalists have held that every kind of land creature has its counterpart in the sea; and taking a broad, general view, that may well be so. But when you come down to particulars — where, for example, does the ocean offer a fish whose temperament matches the wise kindness of the dog? Only the accursed shark can be said, in any general way, to bear some comparison to him.

True, landsmen in general have always looked on the native inhabitants of the seas with feelings unspeakably unsociable and repellent. We know the sea to be an everlasting terra incognita, so much so that Columbus sailed over countless unknown worlds to discover his one superficial western one. By far the most terrible of all mortal disasters have, since time immemorial, fallen on tens and hundreds of thousands of those who have gone to sea, without distinction. And only a moment's thought will show that however much baby man may boast of his science and skill, and however much that science and skill may grow in a flattering future, the sea will go on insulting and murdering him forever and ever, to the crack of doom, and pulverizing the stateliest, stiffest frigate he can build. Yet for all that, the constant repetition of these very impressions has made man lose the sense of the sea's full awfulness that originally belongs to it.

The first boat we read of floated on an ocean that with Portuguese vengeance had drowned a whole world without leaving so much as a widow. That same ocean rolls now. That same ocean destroyed the wrecked ships of last year. Yes, foolish mortals — Noah's flood has not yet subsided. Two thirds of the fair world it still covers.

How do the sea and the land differ, that a miracle upon one is not a miracle upon the other? Supernatural terrors seized the Hebrews when under the feet of Korah and his company the living ground opened and swallowed them up forever. Yet not a modern sun ever sets without the living sea swallowing up ships and crews in precisely the same manner.

But the sea is not only the enemy of man, who is a stranger to it; it is also a fiend to its own offspring — worse than the Persian host who murdered his own guests, it does not spare even the creatures it has spawned itself. Like a savage tigress thrashing in the jungle who rolls over on her own cubs and smothers them, the sea dashes even the mightiest whales against the rocks and leaves them there beside the split wrecks of ships. No mercy, no power but its own, governs it. Panting and snorting like a mad warhorse that has lost its rider, the masterless ocean overruns the globe.

Consider the subtlety of the sea — how its most dreaded creatures glide under water, invisible for the most part, treacherously hidden beneath the loveliest shades of blue. Consider also the devilish brilliance and beauty of many of its most merciless species, like the elegantly shaped bodies of many kinds of sharks. Consider, once more, the universal cannibalism of the sea, all of whose creatures prey upon each other, waging eternal war since the world began.

Consider all this, and then turn to this green, gentle, and most docile earth. Consider them both — the sea and the land — and do you not find a strange parallel to something in yourself? For as this appalling ocean surrounds the green land, so in the soul of man there lies one island Tahiti, full of peace and joy, but surrounded by all the horrors of the half-known life. God keep you! Do not push off from that island — you can never return!
